At the same time, Secretary of Agriculture Benson has pointed out that the United States cannot afford to allow outside farm products to come into the United States to compete with the United States products held at subsidized prices. Not only is the United States stealing our markets, but she is closing her
Supply-Agriculture
markets to us. It is obvious that we are being placed in a very difficult squeeze.
The United States is bartering much of her surplus agricultural products of various kinds, not only grain. Since permission was given last year to Secretary Benson to barter, more than $82 million worth of commodities have been exported to 23 countries in exchange for imports valued at $53 million. Look at what has happened there. Some $82 million worth of products have been bartered for commodities valued at only $53 million. In other words the United States has lost the difference between $53 million and $82 million in value, and she has done that in order to get rid of surplus products, which shows how serious her competition is for Canada; and it will become more serious. The surplus products which she has been bartering include corn, flaxseed, grain sorghum, cottonseed oil, barley, oats and cotton. The countries with which she has bartered include Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Turkey, Yugoslavia, England, Ireland, Scotland, Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, India, Formosa, Japan, Korea, Colombia, Peru, which is enough to show at how many points the United States is impinging on possible Canadian external markets.
What can we do to resist the pressure of a nation like that? The United States financial and economic strength is so great that she will be able to force her surpluses into world markets to a tremendous degree because she has such an enormous population. She also has vast resources; she has great industrial strength; she has great financial strength, every one of which is superior to the greatest degree. We have hardly any chance at all to compete.
The only way Canada could hope to compete with the United States in foreign markets under circumstances like that would be for Canada to adopt a scheme for using her national credit, similar to that which Japan employed in 1933. That is a possible solution. There will be those who will begin to wonder whether or not the proposal I am making here is sound. I point out that Japan used this scheme in 1933. What did she do? I am not going to go into detail at the present time. Later I may tell the committee something about the achievements and the methods Japan used whereby she was able to put her products into foreign markets at prices utterly impossible for them to compete with.

Supply-Agriculture
Meanwhile, is there open to us any procedure other than forcing our surpluses into export markets? I believe that even trying to use our national credit, as Japan did, would hardly strengthen us enough to compete successfully with the United States. The United States is going ahead with a rapid production program and has accumulated surpluses right along, which she feels she must do.
Could the United States have so managed her stores of grain that they would have occasioned her no serious embarrassment? Is there any reason why the grain in the United States should be in those ships, or why she should have to pay storage for it? That is the question we have to ask ourselves. Could the United States have had all her surpluses safely stored on her farms without storage costs to her national government? I believe that could have been done, and that we in Canada can do it, and this would seem to offer a part of the way out of our difficulties. I suggest this should have been done in the United States.
Mark you, I am coming to the United States now, so we do not have to argue about the situation in Canada. If it would seem to work over there, we might consider whether it could work here. Suppose the United States had bought the grain, we will say, from a farmer in Montana. Let us say that the farmer produced 5,000 bushels of grain, and the United States said to this farmer: We will give you the money, or we will lend you the money with which to build on your farm approved farm storage. Then you store your grain in the storage on your farm and we will pay you the money for that grain just as though you had it in an elevator. Then the grain will be our grain in your storage. To recompense you for the efforts you put forth in looking after that grain we will pay you, say, 10 per cent of that grain every year as storage. Therefore at the end of 10 years, if we do not take that grain off your hands, if we cannot sell it or cannot use it, then at the end of the 10-year period you will own the grain. It then will be your grain stored on your farm under your storage. Then in one more year, we will pay you the value of the storage facilities.
Then that farmer would have on his farm that 5,000 bushels of grain, which unless the government called for it would be his grain, and he would consequently take care of it. At the same time it would be available for the United States to take at any time she felt she needed it, because she had already paid him for it. I am not going into too many details in regard to the matter, but I believe people can get the general idea of it. Let us see if that is not a possible solution.

The important thing is not to have that grain on the government's hands. The hon. member for Meadow Lake should be thinking a lot about this. I suggest to him that it is a solution. He should be thinking about what I am saying. This may be a serious thing, as at present it is costing the United States $1 million a day for her stored wheat and corn. I tell you that we in Canada do not want any burdens of that sort on our shoulders. If there is a way by which we can store the grain and have it taken care of on our farms, thereby avoiding the public expense of storing the grain, and still have the grain in case we need it, then that is what we want.
I submit that in a general way my suggestion will solve the problem, because any man who has a good supply of wheat on his farm will treasure it very highly. He knows how valuable the wheat will be on his farm if he owns it. He needs the storage facilities and if he had it and in it the wheat it would be a valuable thing for him. He would not have the right to sell that wheat until the government gave him permission to do so. He would feel pretty well supported, would he not, having a store of wheat on that basis? That sort of storage would alleviate the situation in the United States at the present time with regard to all the surplus which is turning them into a frenzy. If surpluses were safely stored thus on individual farms and being taken care of by the farmers, then the problems of storage space and of storage costs would be solved for the government.
As far as I can see, Mr. Chairman, the only way of taking care of our surpluses in such a manner that we shall not have to curtail our production is to store the grain on our farms with people who know how valuable such commodities are, and who will have cause to do a good job. Just think of what a blessing it would be to the flood-stricken areas of Saskatchewan if the farmers there had a store of grain of various kinds and other kinds of farm commodities on their farms. They would have the means to live on their farms. Just think of what a difference it would make in the stricken areas of Manitoba, and in the areas where rust strikes. Look what a difference it would make, not having the farmers in the position that they have to rush their grain into the elevator, and if they cannot get it into an elevator they have to improvise storage on the farm and keep it there, and then have to borrow money on the grain, thereby incurring debt and interest rates and running the risk of having the grain spoiled. As it is now it is exactly as it ought not to be.

I have given a suggestion to show how we can store our grain and other surplus commodities on our farms. If the United States would go one step further and in storing grain on her people's farms would use her national credit, which she could do as Japan did in the thirties, she could pay for the grain on the farms with her credit and it would not cost her a cent. It did not cost the Japanese anything to finance their exports; they used the national credit, which was money, without having to take it away from the taxpayers.
I do not propose to go into all the details of this matter. It is not becoming that I should on this occasion, because it would hardly be in order. Nevertheless there is no use in a member offering a solution if he does not tell how the money can be raised with which to work out that solution.
I wish to go on. If the thing can be done in the United States, if grain and other things can be stored there, they can be stored in Canada just as well.
I have already named six serious dangers which threaten Canadian agriculture. As I have said before, I have indicated how grave is only one of them, namely that of United States competition. Before I elaborate on the other five dangers, which I may or may not do tonight, may I indicate what in my opinion would be the necessary immediate steps to take to protect our Canadian agriculture if Canadian agriculture is to be made stable, as it should be.
We are looking for a solution. Do we want a solution? I wonder if hon. members want a solution, or do they want things to go on in an unstable way. Is there no solution to this problem? Are you prepared to admit that the United States cannot solve this problem, that she has to go on producing herself into strangulation, at the same time strangling the rest of the nations of the world indefinitely? Is there any hon. member who believes that makes sense? Is there any hon. member who believes that it makes sense for the United States to limit her production?
There must be solutions. Let us find them. There is no hint of them except in what I may have said here tonight. There is no hint of them in what the Minister of Finance or any other minister has said. If Canadian agriculture is to be made stable, as it should be and as I believe all thoughtful Canadians desire to see it, then we must begin at the earliest possible moment to take whatever steps are necessary to make it stable.
What are they? I suggest five main measures that Canada, in so far as it is physically possible and desirable, ought to
Supply-Agriculture
adopt for the establishment and maintenance of a sound Canadian agriculture. These five measures are, first, the establishment as soon as it is possible, and it is possible this year, of an adequate system of farm storage of surpluses in approved facilities, paying each farmer for those surpluses in his farm storage and then letting the farmer take care of the grain until the storage that has been paid to him in kind makes the grain his. As I have already indicated, there must be a practical system of farm storage so the farmer does not have to take the rap for everything all the way down the line. That is exactly what he is doing today.
The situation in my constituency is simply deplorable. Men with great collections of grain could not buy even toys for their children last Christmas. I saw two or three of them shedding tears last Christmas when they were telling me the situation they were in. How in the world they ever succeeded in planting crops this spring I do not know. Many of them are just absolutely tied tight with vast amounts of grain on their hands. That is the way they are treating our producers. How can we get sense out of treating our producers like that?
The second suggestion I make is that a system of guaranteed prices be established.

They were happy to throw controls out the window. They challenged this group on occasions, saying that we were in favour of controls and

regimentation and that sort of thing. We were quite happy to take that responsibility. What has been the situation since 1945? The farmers throughout Canada, and particularly western Canada, were trying to recuperate after many years during which they could not replace farm machinery owing to the fact that steel went into the necessities of war.
Then we see what happened. When the first decontrol measure on steel went through, fabricated steel started to go up, in the manufacture of farming machinery. What happened was that farmers' costs in the replacement of farm machinery went up by leaps and bounds, until by 1952 we find that, by and large, agricultural farm machinery was about 200 per cent higher than in 1941. The same thing happened in respect to some agricultural commodities.
It is true that our farm prices went up substantially, but they were always behind the steep increases in prices of the things the farmer had to buy and his general costs of production. The farmer has never asked for unreasonably high prices. He understands without any element of doubt that when things reach their peak, at some point in the inflation period he is going to take the brunt of that inflation, and his prices will fall much faster than his costs of production. So I say that this government-not necessarily the Minister of Agriculture, but the whole government-is responsible for that.
In addition to that, this government, with the right hon. minister as a cabinet minister agreeing with the policy, sold down the river some of the fertilizer plants of this country by which our farmers could have got one item with which they could have maintained soil fertility, at a relatively low cost. This government, as it did with many other things, sold down the river some of our people's fertilizer plants at fire-sale prices. The result has been that the farmer is now paying unduly high prices for his fertilizer ingredients, which in effect are causing a high cost of production figure for the farmer.
This group has gone on record in favour of parity prices. We feel that the Canadian economy is still primarily agricultural. In spite of the fact that we have increased our industrialization, and have developed our natural resources in respect to iron ore, oil and many other minerals, the fact still remains that one of the largest and most important segments of our economy is agriculture. It is rather unfortunate, not only for ourselves but perhaps for the whole free world, that here we have a capitalist government along with other capitalist governments guiding the resources of our country. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South said the

Supply-Agriculture
other day in another debate, when we allow independent or private companies to come in and take our resources, which are not renewable in respect of our minerals, and leave nothing but ghost towns and empty holes from which they have taken the minerals, it is not a conservation program. Indeed it is nothing more than a sort of irresponsible program of capitalism.
Then when we come to agriculture, may I ask what has been done for the conservation of our resources? There are perhaps four main things, Mr. Chairman, that are important in any large-scale agricultural conservation program. One is the soil, one is water, one is our forests and the fourth is our wildlife. Unless we can have a balance of these four important things, we are going to suffer in respect of a program of conservation of these somewhat unrenewable resources. It is true that we can find some ways of renewing them, but unless we have measures to conserve our soil fertility it may well be that the generations now living will not be in such a fortunate condition as that in which we have been, where we have been able to go out in the last century and to break up virgin soil and exploit it.
This government to date, as far as I am concerned, has not taken adequate measures for soil conservation. We have found that over the past years there has been no program of conservation and indeed in many parts of our country this year there are direct indications that this government has not yet thought out a program under which they will enter into agreements with the provinces for adequate soil conservation, adequate land utilization, the drainage of water and the conservation of water resources.
Perhaps the ambit of this problem exceeds that of this department, but I am going to suggest to the minister that he try to get his colleagues to entertain the idea of a national conservation authority by which we can have in Canada the full utilization of our soil, water, forest and wildlife resources. Unless that is done I do not think this government is meeting the problem faced by this country in 1955. We have the condition that a great deal of our soil fertility has been drained off through flooding where there is not adequate drainage so that many thousands -yes, hundreds of thousands-of acres of our best soil are not capable of being brought into production owing to lack of measures for the conservation of that soil and proper drainage and diking projects.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to deal too extensively with trade and parity prices, but to those of us in this group and indeed to all members who rise to speak on agriculture, 
a great many members in this house seem to think we are placing undue emphasis on the condition in respect of agriculture and are perhaps exaggerating the condition when we read from press reports and indeed reports from the dominion bureau of statistics such as the one I have here reported in the Globe and Mail of Thursday, January 6, 1955 to the effect that farm income in 1954 declined about 12J per cent. Then of course we have more particularly a drop in farm income in western Canada of about 46 per cent in the last three years.
I remember, Mr. Chairman, that earlier in the evening the hon. member for Temis-couata was asking the hon. member for Lethbridge certain questions with respect to implements used on farms. One of his questions was whether or not the farmers had adequate farm machinery. In answer to that question, and indeed for the information of the committee, I want to say that agriculture today has not sufficient machinery, nor the type of machinery with which to keep up with its growing needs. Indeed we are finding in agriculture the same situation that exists in all industry. In other words, there is more automation all the time. Even in forage harvesting, as an example, more and more farmers are turning to automatic machinery and new types of equipment such as forage harvesters and new methods by which they put up their forage.
I just want to add that when this government is trying to have a healthy Canadian economy, we do not think the farmer or agriculture should be penalized. I criticize the Minister of Agriculture and his department and the Minister of Trade and Commerce because I do not think it is fair to agriculture that, in order to balance our trade, we should have commodities coming into our country practically free of duty and competing with agricultural products when, on the other hand, we have our agricultural producers obliged to buy in a market in which we have to pay from 20 to 35 and as high as 40 per cent more for articles on which there is a tariff. I refer to things we need on our farms. I say that is not a fair situation.
I know also that in a few days we are going to have brought before us measures to increase tariffs. As a matter of fact a budget resolution was brought in the other day whereby this house was asked to agree to an increase in the tariff on glycol. Hence we have all along the line these things which the farmer has to buy coming in with high tariff duties imposed on them, thereby increasing

the cost to the farmer; whereas on the other hand the farmer is obliged to compete in the open market.
I believe it is true to say that, by and large, at least 95 per cent of the farmers would be quite agreeable to free trade if we had to undertake that sort of program; but I do not believe the Minister of Agriculture or the government of which he is a member is playing fair with the people when the farmer, with regard to the things he has to sell, is asked to compete on the world market, while at the same time he is obliged to buy in a highly protected market. That is not the way by which you can build a healthy Canadian agricultural economy.
When we speak about these matters, if we deal purely with statistics I know they are cold, dead things. But I also know that today tens of thousands of our farmers, their families and their children have not the amenities of life, judged on any basis you want to take, be it that of justice or of good living conditions. In no way can you say that they are in a satisfactory economic bracket. ' We still have tens of thousands of our farmers in the low income bracket, who have not the facilities which we in this day and age regard as the right of every Canadian citizen. The situation is similar in the United States, that great and rich capitalist country. But here in Canada it is our job to try to have an economy by which we can give higher standards of living to our people.
It seems to me that the Minister of Agriculture and the government of which he is a member have been remiss in not understanding that in order to have a healthy economy we must have parity prices for agriculture. In other words we believe the farmers should have guaranteed prices which will return to them a fair share of the national income, in other words a fair price or a price which will have a fair relationship to their cost of production.
Some members of the House of Commons would seem to think such a provision would bankrupt this nation. On the other hand, I maintain that such a program is going to come into operation some day in Canada, and when it does we shall have in this country a healthy economy for more and more people. There can be no contradiction of the statement that the 6,000 unemployed workers in the agricultural implements industry who came here a year ago to meet certain members of the cabinet were unemployed simply because western farmers were not able to buy the farm machinery they needed.
It is true that in some places there are farmers with grain in their bins, a condition

that has come about because of the policy of restricted sales and quotas. They have not been able to sell their grain and have had to store it on their farms at their own risk and expense. I have advocated for a long time in the house that the government should undertake a program of farm storage. On the other hand, the fact remains that when these farmers do have the opportunity to sell their grain they will not get a fair return for it, having in mind the cost of production; and I maintain they are going to find themselves in a most unfair competitive position and will not be able to finance their operations and keep out of debt.
I have here statistics for farm indebtedness covering the years 1937 to 1952. I point out that from 1946 to 1952 farm indebtedness for all Canada increased from $367-9 million to $486 million, and since 1952 it has continued to increase. In other words we are still going into debt in agriculture. Therefore I cannot agree with the hon. member for Lethbridge when he complimented the minister on being a fine minister in respect of the discharge of his departmental responsibilities. I think the minister and the whole government are responsible for the conditions existing today, and I say we are now paying the penalty. A few months ago we had 600,000 unemployed, and the government has seen fit to enter into a program with the provinces in an attempt to find a solution of the unemployment problem. I say these things are a direct result of the poor agricultural policy.
Coming back to the matter of conservation, in my opinion the federal Department of Agriculture should establish an authority which would investigate all the ramifications of agriculture-conservation of water, conservation of soil and, indeed, of forests and wildlife. We would then have an integrated policy for the whole country instead of the hit or miss policy being followed at the present time. The provinces cannot undertake such a policy alone. There must be a national authority working in close cooperation with the provinces.
In another speech the other day I referred to certain conditions in Canada from time to time that are termed national emergencies or disasters, and said that merely to try to cure the cause of one disaster independently is not good enough. I think the time has come when we have to change our perspective so far as the watershed program is concerned, and take a look at what it means interprovincially. In the province of Saskatchewan this year tens of thousands of acres will not be seeded, but I maintain they could

Supply-Agriculture
have been put into production if the government had had the foresight to undertake such a program through a national authority, which should cover the whole watershed of the Assiniboine down through the Qu'Ap-pelle valley into Manitoba, lake Manitoba and lake Winnipeg, and up to the Nelson river.
I maintain such a project should be undertaken. I agree that the Minister of Agriculture is not alone responsible, but he is an important member of the cabinet. Apparently some of his colleagues do not seem to understand the situation but I am sure if he would explain it to them he would get their cooperation to do something along this line.
Finally, in my opinion it is most unfortunate that since 1945 the government has not seen fit to protect agriculture from the ups and downs, which it could well have done if it had had real vision so far as a comprehensive program for agriculture is concerned, a program to provide adequate parity prices for our farmers, adequate storage for surpluses and adequate trade policies by which farm commodities could be sold and our markets maintained.
I believe we have not nearly reached maximum agricultural production in Canada. When the government takes the problems of agriculture as seriously as it does, for example, those concerned with atomic energy and research in that field, and is prepared to spend money to help feed a hungry world, we will have the kind of program of which we can really be proud. We are not making a fight on the home front. Unless we can have an economy in Canada which is universal in its coverage and under which those engaged in agriculture as well as the industrial workers are protected, I think we will lose the important battle the free world is fighting to show the rest of the world that democracy is the best kind of system. The battle is not going to be won merely by vocal propaganda against other kinds of systems. It is going to be won when we can win men's minds. When we do that we will be able to say to the world that we have not only the best political system but also the best economic system, under which we can feed and clothe ourselves, use our resources and conserve them for posterity.
The resources given to us are under stewardship. They are given to us to maintain as stewards; but I maintain that in the past the government has handled them in such a way that they have been exploited and not conserved for the future. We are going to have to pay the price, unless the [Mr. McCullough (Moose Mountain) .3
government is prepared to put forward a comprehensive program for agriculture by which we can really protect the people on our farms today and, indeed, our children's children.

All I can say is that legislation has been announced in Votes and Proceedings today which is intended to deal partially at least with the problem which the farmers are facing because of conditions that have arisen in Manitoba and the northeastern part of Saskatchewan.
I had hoped I might be able to get along some distance with the estimates and that we could have discussed that matter, but that has not been possible. I had intended to be away all next week, but on account of the way the discussion has gone on tonight I shall be back next Thursday and if at all possible will continue this discussion then.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext: The session may be over.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
I-n the meantime I will have a look at the area of the west that is in difficulties, and for the benefit of those who think we should know something about the United States may I say that I shall be meeting Mr. Ezra Benson, secretary of agriculture of the United States, at Regina, in the middle of the area where difficulties exist at the moment. If we get into the details of the estimates next Thursday we can probably have a better discussion then than we might have had tonight. Nevertheless I hope that at the end of next week we will be in a little better humour to try to get along with them, rather than try to hold them up.
We have not accomplished very much tonight, but we have learned some things. I would just like to say to the last speaker that I hope when we take up the estimates again 1 will be able to prove to him that most of the things he had to say tonight are not in accordance with the facts. The main point which bears that out would require only a few words at this time. In the years that

we have been here we have been spending considerable amounts on agriculture, in spite of what has been said. I quite understand that some people may say, "Well you have been spending money, but you have not been getting results." That is not true, either.
Just to indicate that the situation is not exactly as it has been indicated by the last speaker, let me say to him that we were spending around $10 million a year on agriculture when this government took office, and for a short time thereafter. We are now spending around $100 million a year. Some may talk about a dollar being worth half as much as it was back in those earlier years. Even so, it is still a long way from saying there is not more money being spent on agriculture today than ever before.

Supply-Agriculture
hon. friend talks about so much is not very much when compared with what we are spending on agriculture.

Progress reported.

On Monday we shall resume the debate on second reading of the defence production bill, and then go on to Bill No. 3, which refers to international river improvements. Then we shall take the resolution dealing with the amendment to the Municipal Grants Act and, when we finish that, we shall take the second reading of Bill No. 452, respecting loans to fishermen.
Optimistic boy!
It being five minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
